chunks: Al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn Sama'ah, from Abdullah ibn Jabalah, from Ishaq ibn 'Ammar, from Al-Abd al-Salih (peace be upon him), who said:

I asked him: 'If a man from the people of Najran owns land and then converts to Islam, is the khums due upon him according to what the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) made a treaty with them on, or is it according to what is due upon Muslims?' He said: 'The khums is due upon him as it is due upon Muslims, for if they had converted, the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) would not have made a treaty with them.'

key_terms.صَالَحَهُمْ: He made a treaty with them
key_terms.عَلَيْهِ مَا عَلَى: Upon him is what is upon
key_terms.لَمْ يُصَالِحْهُمُ: He did not make a treaty with them

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling of khums on land owned by a person from Najran after they convert to Islam?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies that the specific tax treaty (*Sahm*) granted to the People of Najran was contingent upon their status as *Ahl al-Kitab*; thus, upon their conversion to Islam, their land reverted to the standard Muslim fiscal regime. Shaykh al-Tusi uses this to illustrate the principle that special concessions for non-Muslims do not persist once they join the Muslim community, a key concept in Shia jurisprudence regarding *Kharaj* and *Khums*. The Imam’s reasoning underscores that the Prophet’s agreement was a political and fiscal arrangement for a specific demographic, not a permanent land tenure right.
